title: chroot (1979) and the Idea of a Walled-Off Filesystem
explainer: The chroot system call, added during the development of Version 7 Unix in 1979, let a process see only a restricted subtree of the filesystem, as if that subtree were the entire disk - the first mainstream mechanism for making a program believe it has its own self-contained environment. Decades later, that same idea, layered with process and resource isolation, became the filesystem-isolation piece of what a container is. Building a Docker image uses a direct conceptual descendant of a 1979 Unix feature that was originally meant for build-and-test isolation, not for shipping whole applications.

title: From Google's cgroups to Docker: The Real Lineage of Containers (2006-2013)
explainer: In 2006, Google engineers contributed 'process containers' to the Linux kernel - soon renamed control groups (cgroups) - to limit and account for CPU, memory, and I/O per group of processes. Combined with Linux namespaces, cgroups became the foundation of LXC (2008), a userspace toolkit for running full Linux environments; Docker, launched in 2013, originally built directly on LXC before replacing it with its own runtime. Docker's real innovation wasn't inventing process isolation - it was packaging years of existing kernel-level primitives into an easy image format and workflow that developers actually wanted to use.
